title: Knowing When to Ask: Multi-Signal Calibrated Escalation for LLM Fraud-Investigation Agents
content: Fraud-investigation agents built on large language models are deployed under selective autonomy, closing the routine cases themselves and escalating the difficult ones, because a compliance function cannot accept full automation. That decision is commonly driven by the confidence the agent states about itself, which language models overstate and which a reviewer may accept more readily for coming with a fluent rationale. We build CEG, a calibrated escalation gate over four signals, and use it to measure which of them actually predict when the agent is wrong: stated confidence, self-consistency across repeated independent runs, disagreement with a conventional tabular fraud classifier, and the sufficiency of the evidence retrieved. A calibrator trained on a small labeled development set maps them to the probability that the agent's conclusion is correct, and an asymmetric cost-sensitive rule escalates under an analyst capacity constraint, demanding more certainty to close a case as benign than to conclude fraud. On mobile-money simulator cases, after removing a balance shortcut identified in prior work and with the analyst modeled as an oracle of fixed capacity, three findings stand out. Stated confidence, the signal deployments commonly use, is the weakest gate that is not random, at a calibration error of 0.069 against 0.022 for the combination, and dropping it from the combination changes team cost by 2 units. Disagreement with the classifier carries the gate, and the classifier score alone therefore comes within 12% of the full combination at a fraction of its inference cost. A conformal variant holds its 10% false-negative target within the calibration period and fails it in all ten repetitions once fraud patterns shift, while the share of cases it decides automatically barely moves, so a deployment cannot detect the violation from its own coverage.
